# Project Environment Factors

The forces surrounding a project that determine whether it succeeds, independent of how good the
engineering is. The seminar in [[computer-project-management]] (Topic #12, 15 slides) argues the
strong form of this: most IT projects fail not from technical shortcomings but from an inability to
handle a constantly changing environment.

## The framework stack it uses

| Frame | Distinguishes |
|---|---|
| **PESTLE** | the macro environment — Political, Economical, Sociological, Technological, Legal, Environmental |
| **EEFs vs OPAs** | Enterprise Environmental Factors (the climate you are given) vs Organizational Process Assets (the toolbox you inherit) |
| **Socio-technical model** | projects are driven by people, not by charts and data |
| **PMBOK vs PRINCE2** | a descriptive knowledge base vs a prescriptive methodology |
| **The 4 Ps** | People · Process · Politics · Performance |
| **Brooks' Law** | adding people to a late project makes it later |

The EEF/OPA split is the one that does real work: it separates what a project manager can change
from what must be absorbed. Everything a plan can control lives in OPAs; PESTLE lives entirely in
EEFs.

## Why this sits next to the scheduling pages

The seminar and the labs are deliberately opposite halves of the same course, and the repo says so:

> "Slide 12's *Process* pillar is exactly what the MS Project plan
> delivers; the other three P's (People, Politics, Performance) are what the seminar argues you
> cannot schedule your way out of."
> — Computer Project Management/seminar/README.md, 2026-07-10

That is a sharper claim than it first reads. Of the 4 Ps, the entire apparatus of
[[work-breakdown-structure]], [[critical-path-method]], [[resource-leveling]] and
[[schedule-baseline-and-variance]] addresses exactly one.

**Brooks' Law is the direct connection.** The labs hit a Backend Developer over-allocation and fix
it by resequencing rather than by hiring — [[sequence-integration-after-unit-testing]]. The seminar
supplies the argument for why that is the right instinct: communication overhead grows
non-linearly, so the extra head does not buy proportional throughput. Two artefacts in one repo,
one supplying the reason for the other's choice, without either cross-referencing it.

## Toxic environments, named

Slide 9 names three anti-patterns as things to steer clear of — *Death March*, *Adrenaline
Junkies*, *Template Zombies* — and slide 10 turns them into recommendations: embrace change,
dismantle toxic cultures, monitor the environment, retrain project managers. Slide 6 argues the
related point that "freezing" requirements fails under a dynamic ICT environment, and that
conceptual integrity has to be maintained *through* change rather than by preventing it.
